title: Addressing the global cirrhosis epidemic: one size will not fit all.
text_summary: 本文评论了全球肝硬化流行现状及"一刀切"防控策略的局限性。肝硬化为全球第11大死因，病因谱在不同地区差异显著(病毒性肝炎、酒精、NAFLD)。文章呼吁针对不同地区的肝硬化病因谱制定差异化的筛查、预防和治疗策略，强调NAFLD相关肝硬化在发达国家的快速增长趋势。

Addressing the global cirrhosis epidemic: one size will not 
fit all
Cirrhosis is a global health concern, as the 11th most 
common cause of mortality worldwide that accounts 
for 2% of deaths annually.1 The causes of cirrhosis are 
largely secondary to public health and lifestyle-related 
exposures, including hepatitis B and C, alcohol-related 
liver disease, and non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). 
Therefore, cirrhosis epidemiology could be influenced 
by interventions targeted at reducing these conditions. 
Over the past several decades, regional and international 
efforts to mitigate cirrhosis risk factors have been 
developed, including WHO resolutions to eliminate viral 
hepatitis by 2030, reduce harmful alcohol consumption, 
and tackle the obesity epidemic by promoting physical 
activity and a healthy diet. To assess the efficacy of these 
efforts on cirrhosis disease burden and to inform future 
health policy initiatives, the availability of contemporary 
epidemiological data is paramount, especially data that 
are stratified by cirrhosis cause and region.
In 
The 
Lancet 
Gastroenterology 
& 
Hepatology, 
the Global Burden of Disease Study (GBD) 2017 
Cirrhosis Collaborators present data that advance 
our understanding of the changing epidemiology of 
cirrhosis and chronic liver diseases around the world.2 
Although the absolute number of cirrhosis-related 
deaths increased from 899 000 (95% uncertainty 
interval [UI] 829 000–948 000) in 1990 to 1·32 million 
(1·27–1·45) in 2017, the age-standardised death rate 
decreased from 21·0 (95% UI 19·2–22·3) per 100 000 
in 1990 to 16·5 (15·8–18·1) per 100 000 in 2017. This 
observation is attributed in part to an ageing global 
population; however, data from this study also suggest 
that improvements have been made to medical 
care for patients with liver disease in high-income 
countries. Conversely, the age-standardised prevalence 
of compensated cirrhosis increased by approximately 
3% and that of decompensated cirrhosis increased by 
approximately 20%. Therefore, although improvements 
in mortality rates are encouraging, the increase in 
cirrhosis prevalence underscores the need for ongoing 
efforts to prevent cirrhosis incidence and associated 
morbidity.
The study by the GBD 2017 Cirrhosis Collaborators 
identified differential epidemiological trends on the 
basis of both disease cause and region. With respect 
to viral hepatitis, the proportion of hepatitis B-related 
deaths was highest in western sub-Saharan Africa, 
whereas hepatitis C-related mortality was highest in 
Asia and north Africa and the Middle East. Conversely, 
alcohol-related deaths were highest in Europe, Latin 
America, and the Caribbean. Deaths secondary to 
NASH, the fastest growing cause of cirrhosis and the 
only one not to show a decrease in age-standardised 
death rates overall, were highest in Latin America and 
high-income Asia Pacific. Finally, these data highlight 
a concerning trend in high-income North America,3,4 
where cirrhosis mortality over the study period shifted 
to younger age groups compared with age-related 
trends in other regions.
The limitations of the methods inherent to the 
design of GBD must be recognised. Firstly, cause of 
death is defined by International Classification of 
Diseases, version 10 (ICD-10), coding. Although ICD-10 
codes for cirrhosis and decompensation events have 
been validated in data from the USA5 and Canada,6 
the accuracy in other regions or of the use of other 
chronic liver disease codes are unknown. Furthermore, 
codes for hepatocellular carcinoma, which almost 
exclusively occur in individuals with cirrhosis, were not 
included. Therefore, the overall burden of cirrhosis is

likely to be underestimated. Secondly, the definition 
of cirrhosis cause was not based on individual data but 
was determined using statistical modelling to assign a 
proportion of cirrhosis cases from a specific region to a 
cause. This model was calculated from the proportion of 
cirrhosis cases suspected to be secondary to hepatitis B 
or C, alcohol-related liver disease, NASH, or other causes 
in a particular region based on the proportion of liver 
cancers in that region with HBsAg seroprevalence and 
hepatitis C virus antibody positivity, alcohol use per 
capita, and obesity prevalence. This model assumes 
that each cause results in equal rates of cirrhosis 
mortality, which might be an oversimplification. 
Finally, prevalence for compensated and decom­
pensated cirrhosis was determined using codes from 
both inpatient and outpatient claims, in which those 
admitted to hospital with a primary diagnosis of 
cirrhosis were considered to be decompensated and 
all others were considered to be compensated. This 
approach has not been validated and might explain 
why a disproportionately greater increase in prevalence 
of decompensated cirrhosis versus compensated 
cirrhosis was seen, because prevalence was calculated 
using hospital data only. Therefore, regional data with 
the ability to define both cirrhosis cause and outcomes 
with known and adequate accuracy will be important 
adjuncts to this work.
Overall, these results provide an essential step in 
our evolving understanding of global liver disease 
epidemiology. Of note, they emphasise that the 
development of chronic disease prevention and 
management strategies for liver disease and cirrhosis 
are unlikely to succeed with a universal one-size-fits-all 
approach.

Extracting the benefits of berberine for colorectal cancer
Colorectal cancer was the third most common 
cancer and the second leading cause of cancer 
death worldwide in 2018. Although screening for 
colorectal cancer and precancerous adenomatous 
polyps (adenomas) has been successful in reducing 
colorectal cancer mortality, there are barriers to 
widespread implementation, associated harms, and 
inherent limitations to efficacy. Thus, novel strategies 
for prevention remain an important unmet need. 
Chemoprevention, defined as the use of agents 
(eg, medications, vitamins, or supplements) for the 
inhibition, delay, or reversal of carcinogenesis, is an 
appealing alternative or complement to screening, 
particularly in resource-limited settings. In 2016, 
the US Preventive Services Task Force recommended 
low-dose aspirin for the prevention of cardiovascular 
events and colorectal cancer in certain age groups 
with specific cardiovascular risk profiles.1 However, 
concerns regarding potential adverse effects of aspirin 
have sustained interest in additional chemopreventive 
agents, including natural products such as berberine, 
an isoquinoline quaternary alkaloid extracted from 
many medicinal plants.

used for its perceived antimicrobial and antidiarrhoeal 
properties in Ayurvedic and Chinese medicine for
